title: Business, user and supplier interests
blurb: Describe the three project interests and say which project board role represents each one.
question: Staff who will maintain a new system after handover belong to which project interest, and which board role represents them?

teach.body: Formally: PRINCE2 focuses on three principal categories of project stakeholder, the business, user and supplier interests, and includes them in the project's governance and management arrangements. In plain English: every project has someone paying for a result, someone who will use the result, and someone who will build it. All three need a voice where decisions are made.

teach.h: The three interests at a glance
head: Interest
Main concern
Board role
rows: Meets a business need; stays value for money
Products meet requirements and give benefits
Skills and knowledge to deliver the products
teach.caption: The business need must be justified continuously, not just at the start.

root.label: User interest
root.sub: help define requirements and check they are met

children.label: End users, impacted staff
children.sub: and those who operate or maintain the products

children.label: External end users
children.sub: or people impacted by the outputs

teach.caption: Users are not only the people at the keyboard: operators and maintainers count too.

teach.h: Suppliers can be internal or external
teach.caption: 'Supplier' means whoever has the skills to deliver, not just an outside company.

teach.h: Why all three must be heard
teach.body: Each interest pulls a different way. The business wants value for money, users want products that work for them, and suppliers need realistic demands they can resource. Putting all three on the project board means trade-offs are made openly by people with the authority to commit their side, instead of one interest overruling the others.

head: Board role
Interest
How many?
teach.caption: Large user or supplier communities may need several representatives; the business has a single executive.

teach.h: Worked scenario: an outpatient booking app
teach.body: Fenwick Valley Health Trust is building a patient booking app. Finance director Martin Osei is executive: he must show the app stays value for money. Head of outpatients Grace Lyle is senior user, speaking for clinic staff and for patients, who are users outside the trust. Two senior suppliers sit on the board: the trust's digital lead, Imran Bashir, and the app developer's director, Elena Ruiz, because both organizations deliver parts of the product.

teach.text: Trap: the business INTEREST is not the business LAYER. The business layer commissions the project from outside the project management team; the business interest is represented inside it, on the board, by the executive. Second trap: suppliers can be in-house, and users can be outside the business.

rows.label: Is this still worth the money?
Will ward staff find the rota usable?
Can the products be maintained after handover?
Do we have engineers with the right skills?

items: Business: meets a business need, continuously justified as value for money; executive.
User: uses, operates, maintains or is impacted by the products; senior user(s).
Supplier: has the skills and knowledge to deliver, internal or external; senior supplier(s).
One executive; senior user and senior supplier roles may be held by several people.

summary: You can now describe the business, user and supplier interests and name the board role that represents each. You can also spot users and suppliers on both sides of the organization's boundary.

A.q: Which project board role represents the business interest?
options: Senior user
Executive
Senior supplier
Project manager
A.why: The executive represents the business interest and is accountable for continued business justification (6.2.1).

whyNot.0: The senior user represents the user interest.
whyNot.2: The senior supplier represents the supplier interest.
whyNot.3: The project manager is at the managing level and is not a board member.

A.q: Which interest is concerned that the project stays value for money throughout its life?
options: The user interest
The supplier interest
The commissioning interest
The business interest
A.why: The business interest requires the project to meet a business need that is continuously justified as value for money.

whyNot.0: The user interest is about requirements being specified and met.
whyNot.1: The supplier interest is about having the skills and resources to deliver.
whyNot.2: Commissioning is the business layer's job, not one of the three project interests.

A.q: Which person belongs to the user interest?
options: A technician who will maintain the new equipment
The contractor's engineer building the equipment
The executive securing funding for the project
The project manager planning the next stage
A.why: Users include those who will use, operate, maintain or be impacted by the products.

whyNot.1: The contractor's engineer has the skills to deliver, so belongs to the supplier interest.
whyNot.2: The executive represents the business interest.
whyNot.3: The project manager manages the project on behalf of the board; they do not represent an interest.

B.q:
Which two statements about the project interests are correct?
1. Users can sit outside the business.
2. Suppliers must be external organizations.
3. More than one person may represent users.
4. The senior supplier represents the business interest.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
B.why: Users can be inside or outside the business (1), and the senior user role may be held by more than one person (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: suppliers can come from within the organization.
whyNot.1: Both are false: suppliers can be internal, and the executive represents the business.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: the senior supplier represents the supplier interest.

B.q: A council's in-house IT department will build a new parking permit system. How is the IT department's interest represented on the board?
options: By a senior user
By the executive
By a senior supplier
By the business layer
B.why: Suppliers may come from within the organization. Whoever brings the skills to deliver is represented by a senior supplier.

whyNot.0: The senior user represents those who will use or be affected by the system.
whyNot.1: The executive represents the business interest, not the people building the product.
whyNot.3: The business layer commissions the project and sits outside the project management team.

B.q: Which statement about the user interest is correct?
options: Users secure the funding and own the business case
Users help define requirements and check they are met
Users commit the skills and resources to build products
Users set the project-level tolerances for the board
B.why: The user interest supports both defining the product requirements and making sure those requirements are met.

whyNot.0: Securing funding and owning the business case is the executive's job.
whyNot.2: Committing skills and resources to build products is the supplier interest.
whyNot.3: Project-level tolerances are set by the business layer.

C.q: Ward nurses will use a rostering system built by an external software firm. Who represents each group on the project board?
options: Senior user for the nurses; senior supplier for the firm
Executive for the nurses; senior supplier for the firm
Senior user for the nurses; executive for the firm
Senior supplier for the nurses; senior user for the firm
C.why: The nurses will use the product, so the senior user represents them; the firm delivers it, so a senior supplier represents it.

whyNot.1: The executive represents the business interest, not the users.
whyNot.2: The firm is a supplier; the executive represents the business.
whyNot.3: The roles are reversed: users are represented by the senior user.

C.q: Which interest is concerned with whether the products can be built with the skills available, and which board role represents it?
options: User; senior user (one or more)
Business; executive (exactly one)
Supplier; team manager
Supplier; senior supplier
C.why: The supplier interest brings the skills and knowledge to deliver the products and is represented by the senior supplier.

whyNot.0: The user interest is about requirements and benefits, not delivery skills.
whyNot.1: The business interest is about the business need and value for money.
whyNot.2: The interest is right, but team managers work at the delivering level and are not board members.

C.q: Why does PRINCE2 include all three interests in the project's governance?
options: So the business layer can leave direction to the users
So each interest can set its own stage tolerances
So decisions balance value, usability and deliverability
So the supplier can approve the business case
C.why: Including business, user and supplier in governance means decisions weigh value for money, user needs and the ability to deliver.

whyNot.0: The board, not the users, directs the project within the remit set by the business layer.
whyNot.1: Stage tolerances are set by the project board as a whole.
whyNot.3: The executive owns the business case for the business interest.

reteach.title: A wedding cake has three interests
reteach.question: Who has a stake in a wedding cake: the people paying, the guests eating it, or the baker?

blocks.body: The couple paying want value for money (business). The guests want a cake they enjoy (user). The baker needs a design they can actually make (supplier). A good cake meets all three. A PRINCE2 project board brings the same three voices together: executive, senior user and senior supplier.

blocks.text: The baker could be a family member (internal supplier) and some guests may be strangers (users outside the business): the interests are about roles, not about which organization people belong to.

explain.body: Projects are created to meet a business need, which must be continuously justified as value for money. The executive represents this view.

test.q: What does the business interest focus on?
options: How easy the products are to use
Continued value for money
The skills to build the products
Day-to-day team management
test.why: The business interest needs the project to be continuously justified as value for money.

whyNot.0: Ease of use is a user concern.
whyNot.2: Delivery skills are the supplier interest.
whyNot.3: Day-to-day management is the project manager's job, not an interest.

explain.body: Users will use, operate, maintain or be impacted by the products. They may be inside or outside the business. The senior user represents them.

test.q: Which person is part of the user interest?
options: The contractor's site manager on the build
The supplier's quality manager for the plant
The project manager running the stage
An engineer who will maintain the plant
test.why: Those who will maintain the products are users.

whyNot.0: The contractor's site manager is part of the supplier interest.
whyNot.1: The supplier's quality manager is part of the supplier interest.
whyNot.2: The project manager manages the project; they do not represent an interest.

explain.body: Suppliers have the skills and knowledge to deliver the products. They may come from inside the organization or be external. The senior supplier represents them.

test.q: Which statement about suppliers is correct?
options: They may be internal or external
They must be external companies
They are represented by the executive
They sit in the business layer
test.why: Suppliers can come from within the organization or be external.

whyNot.2: The executive represents the business interest.
whyNot.3: The business layer commissions the project; suppliers are represented on the board.

explain.body: There is exactly one executive. The senior user and senior supplier roles may each be held by more than one person when user or supplier communities are large or complex.

test.q: How many people may represent the user interest on the project board?
options: Exactly one senior user
None, as the executive covers it
One or more senior users
Two, one internal and one external
test.why: Depending on the scale and complexity of the user community, more than one person may represent users.

whyNot.0: Exactly one applies to the executive, not the senior user.
whyNot.1: The user interest must be represented on the board by the senior user.
whyNot.3: There is no fixed number of two; it depends on the user community.
